strengths: Addresses a practically important problem in LLM-based influence estimation with clear computational motivation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 models, 3 influence methods, 8 GLUE datasets with 10 random seeds and robust pairwise comparison methodology
Provides formal theoretical counterexample (Theorem 5.1) to prior cancellation effect claims
Proposes practical aggregation strategies (Vote method) with consistent improvements and useful NDR metric for avoiding expensive fine-tuning
Well-executed experiments with extensive ablations, detailed appendices, and clear presentation
weaknesses: Core finding that middle layers outperform embeddings is somewhat expected given transformer architecture; limited novelty overall
Highly inconsistent results across models—Llama-3.2 1B dramatically underperforms (often worse than random baseline) with inadequate explanation, raising serious generalization concerns

Evaluation methodology has significant limitations: synthetic label noise (artificial), reduced dataset size (4500 samples for efficiency), weak Random baseline comparison, and assumptions not validated as optimal for influence

NDR/AUC metric validation overstated—Table 2 shows only moderate correlations (0.4-0.9, median 0.5-0.7) contradicting claims of 'strong predictive capability'; Vote aggregation inflation of correlations is somewhat circular
Theorem 5.1 provides existence proof but lacks characterization of when/why cancellation helps; remark acknowledges cases where it hurts, weakening the claim
Limited scope: only gradient-based methods, only classification with label noise, only GLUE tasks, only LoRA fine-tuning—generalization to other settings unclear
Vote aggregation shows consistent degradation on COLA dataset; parameter k choice appears arbitrary; computational costs not discussed; only 10 runs may be underpowered for statistical testing

Missing critical analysis: no explanation for Llama failure mode despite clear evidence (Figure 20 shows uniform noise distribution), no investigation of why layer preferences vary across model sizes, no deeper characterization of when findings hold

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 models, 3 influence methods, 8 datasets, and 10 seeds
Directly challenges seminal prior work with both theoretical and empirical evidence
Extensive documentation with detailed ablations and appendices supporting reproducibility
Vote aggregation method shows consistent improvements with strong correlations (0.8-0.9) to downstream performance in some settings
Practical insights about layer-specific signal complementarity and the limitations of averaging
weaknesses: Highly inconsistent results across models and tasks: RoBERTa shows embedding layers work best for TracIn, contradicting main claims; Llama-3.2 shows influence methods underperform random baseline across most configurations

Limited novelty: proposed aggregation methods (Rank, Vote) are straightforward heuristics; NDR is a standard metric; theoretical result is a constructive counterexample without characterization of when it applies
Weak theoretical contribution: Theorem 5.1 only shows a counterexample exists; provides no explanation for why middle layers perform better empirically or prediction of layer performance

Overclaimed findings relative to evidence: NDR correlations of 0.5-0.7 are moderate not 'reliable'; claim 'middle layers are better estimators' contradicted by RoBERTa results and task-dependent variation

Artificial evaluation design: synthetic label noise may not reflect real data quality issues; 30% filtering rate is arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; uses indirect proxy (task accuracy) rather than validating influence estimates are correct
Results suggest aggregation method matters more than layer choice (Vote shows much stronger NDR correlations than layer selection), which contradicts the paper's emphasis on layer choice
Only evaluated on GLUE NLU tasks with synthetic noise; generalization to other domains, real-world noise patterns, and other training scenarios unclear

Methodological concerns: non-standard embedding compression preprocessing; proprietary models limit reproducibility; no code availability mentioned; multiple comparisons without statistical correction
Paper addresses four research questions simultaneously, diluting focus and making contributions feel scattered across too many threads
Critical failure inadequately addressed: Llama-3.2 complete failure vs random baseline suggests fundamental limitations of the approach that merit investigation rather than dismissal

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study with rigorous experimental design across multiple models (4 LLMs), datasets (8 GLUE tasks), influence methods (3 variants), and proper statistical testing (10 runs, Wilcoxon tests)
Valuable theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1) providing a counterexample to Yeh et al. (2022), challenging the reliability of the cancellation effect metric
Practical contributions including proposed Rank and Vote aggregation strategies and the NDR metric that enables influence function evaluation without expensive retraining
Well-motivated research addressing genuine gaps in understanding which layers are optimal for influence estimation in LLMs, with clear practical implications
Thorough presentation with extensive supplementary materials, clear methodology, appropriate visualizations, and reproducible experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Rank and Vote aggregations are straightforward heuristics lacking deep theoretical justification; NDR is simply a counting metric without sophisticated innovation

Concerning generalization issues with model-dependent inconsistencies: Llama-3.2 1B fundamentally fails (performs worse than random baseline on most tasks), layer preferences vary substantially across models, and inconsistencies are inadequately explained or addressed

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Theorem 5.1 shows high cancellation *can* improve performance but provides no insight into *when/why* this occurs; no theoretical explanation for why middle layers should be better; missing mechanistic understanding

Modest practical improvements with mixed results: Vote aggregation gains typically 1-3% with many statistically insignificant; NDR correlations moderate (0.5-0.8); CoLA and QQP show consistent degradation; improvements appear task/method-dependent

Limited evaluation scope with artificial experimental setup: synthetic noise (20% random label flips) doesn't reflect realistic corruption; evaluation on only small GLUE tasks may not generalize to large-scale pretraining; no computational cost analysis; 30% filtering threshold somewhat contrived

Insufficient investigation of failure modes and design choices: Llama's systematic underperformance explained only by noise distribution histograms (unsatisfying); different influence methods show inconsistent layer preferences without analysis; checkpoint selection via validation loss unjustified; filtering/noise levels not ablated

Model generalization concerns: Only 4 similar, relatively recent architectures tested; no evaluation on older models (BERT, GPT-2) or other families (T5); results may be specific to instruction-tuned LLaMA-era models

Presentation could be more focused: Paper addresses four distinct RQs making it feel scattered; important negative results (Llama failure) under-emphasized; missing intuition for why findings hold (e.g., why attention layers > embeddings)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (RoBERTa, Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and datasets (8 GLUE tasks) with 10 random seeds, demonstrating thorough empirical rigor
Theoretical contribution: Theorem 5.1 provides formal counterexample showing cancellation effect can improve (not harm) influence estimation, refuting prior claims by Yeh et al. 2022
Practical solutions addressing real bottlenecks: NDR metric enables influence evaluation without expensive model retraining; Vote aggregation provides consistent (1-3%) improvements
Strong reproducibility: detailed methodology, extensive appendices with noise distributions and layer rankings, promised open-source code
Well-structured analysis of four research questions with both theoretical and empirical evidence
weaknesses: Inconsistent results across models undermine generalizability: Llama-3.2 1B frequently fails to outperform random baseline (Appendix M); RoBERTa shows best performance on later layers, contradicting title claim; inconsistency inadequately explained

Incremental novelty: core finding (middle layers often better) advances understanding incrementally; limited mechanistic insight into why middle layers work; connection to knowledge editing literature mentioned but not explored

Modest practical impact: Vote aggregation improves performance by only 1-3% and introduces hyperparameter k requiring tuning (k∈[10,50]); NDR metric shows moderate correlations (0.5-0.7, improving to 0.8-0.9 only with Vote—creating circularity)

Methodological concerns: synthetically injected label noise may not reflect real-world patterns; checkpoint selection based on lowest validation loss could introduce bias; embedding compression modifies influence function inputs; unfair comparison with Yeh et al. using different models/settings
Limited scope: only GLUE classification and instruction-following tasks; open-ended generation untested; only LoRA fine-tuning evaluated; findings may not generalize beyond these settings
Theorem 5.1 shows counterexample but does not establish cancellation is generally unreliable; proof requires specific assumptions about gradient directions potentially unrealistic in practice
Vote aggregation complexity: hyperparameter k varies significantly with model/method/layer (Appendix L), undermining simplicity claims relative to mean aggregation
Insufficient analysis of mechanisms: why middle layers encode noise better than embeddings/output layers remains unclear; Appendix K's sample influence ranking analysis superficial
